n: This lecture is devoted to the systemic inflammatory response syndrome. SIRS is a non-specific, excessively amplified defensive response triggered by infectious or non-infectious stressors. In trauma, SIRS is regarded as an independent predictor of death. By increasing susceptibility to infection, it can lead to multiple organ dysfunction syndrome, that is, MODS. The lecture outline has 6 sections: definition and triggers; cells and mediators; endothelium and coagulation; mtDAMPs; lung morphology, that is, DAD and ARDS; biomarkers and treatment. Expected outcome: to explain the pathogenesis of SIRS and to list the stages of diffuse alveolar damage in the lung: exudative, proliferative and fibrotic.

Definition of SIRS and its triggers. SIRS is a non-specific, excessively amplified defensive response to infectious or non-infectious stressors. Trigger groups: infectious, that is, microbial invasion and sepsis; non-infectious injury, that is, trauma, burns and surgery; other non-infectious causes, that is, ischaemia-reperfusion and tumour. In infectious SIRS, PAMPs, that is, pathogen-associated molecular patterns, play the role; in traumatic SIRS, mainly DAMPs, that is, damage-associated molecular patterns. Attention: SIRS is not sepsis; SIRS can develop even in the absence of infection.

t: Difference between local and systemic response
n: Difference between local and systemic response. A minor injury causes a local defensive reaction, whereas an extensive injury causes a response of a systemic nature. Together with activation of the immune system, a neurohormonal response is also triggered: corticotropin, cortisol and catecholamines are released. In controlled inflammation, anti-inflammatory cytokines are formed and the signs of inflammation gradually subside. If the factor is strong and the organism is weak, mediators pass into the circulation and damage distant tissues as well. This clinical picture is called SIRS.

t: From inflammation to SIRS: the chain of stages
n: Let us consider the chain of stages from inflammation to SIRS. If the factor is strong and the organism is weak, proinflammatory mediators pass into the general bloodstream. As a result, the endothelium is damaged in distant tissues. Cytokines disrupt the endothelium, coagulation increases while fibrinolysis decreases, that is, the balance of coagulation and fibrinolysis changes. Thrombosis appears in the microcirculation. Consequently, DIC, that is, disseminated intravascular coagulation, and MODS, that is, multiple organ dysfunction syndrome, are observed.

t: Case analysis: a patient with burn disease
n: Case analysis. Situation: after a severe burn, burn disease develops, that is, local and general changes, together with SIRS. DAMPs, that is, damage-associated molecular patterns, are released from the burned tissue and activate macrophages, and mediators increase. Blood volume and cardiac output fall, blood hypercoagulation, that is, DIC, and hypoperfusion appear: diuresis decreases and consciousness changes. Question: which mediators and signs are linked? Patients with high HMGB-1 and IL-10 on admission did not survive.

The cytokine “storm” activates macrophages, neutrophils, dendritic cells and the endothelium. Activation of the TLR, that is, the Toll-like receptor, increases synthesis of TNF-α, IL-1, IL-6, IL-8 and IL-12. The role of effector cells is given in the table: the neutrophil arrives within minutes and produces ROS; the macrophage arrives within hours and releases TNF-α and IL-1; the dendritic cell is activated through TLR and releases cytokines; the endothelium forms adhesion proteins and TF. Excess cytokines and ROS, that is, reactive oxygen species, damage organs.

Pro- and anti-inflammatory mediators. When Toll-like receptors are activated, tumour necrosis factor TNF-α, as well as IL-1, IL-6, IL-8 and IL-12, increase. There is also negative feedback: Th2 lymphocytes produce IL-10 and IL-13, and cytokine inhibitors appear in the blood. Inhibitors: soluble receptors, that is, sTNFR I, II and sIL-1R II, and the IL-1 receptor antagonist, IL-1ra. In the Th1 response, the cytokines IFN-γ, IL-2 and LT-α enhance inflammation, while IFN-γ and IL-12 direct it. In the Th2 response, the cytokines IL-4, IL-5 and IL-10 suppress Th1 cytokines, and IFN-γ prevents differentiation.

t: SIRS, CARS and MARS: loss of balance
n: SIRS, CARS and MARS are three manifestations of loss of balance. SIRS is generalised inflammation that develops when anti-inflammatory mechanisms are insufficient; in it, inflammatory factors are hyperactive. Attention: SIRS is not CARS. CARS is an excessive anti-inflammatory response leading to immunosuppression. MARS, that is, mixed antagonist response syndrome, is a state in which hyperactivity and immunosuppression alternate periodically; in it, MODS, septic shock and anergy are observed.

Quick questions on cytokines and syndromes. First question: which anti-inflammatory cytokines can Th2 lymphocytes produce? Second question: how do CARS and MARS differ from each other? Remember that SIRS is not CARS. Third question: which soluble receptors and which antagonist are examples of cytokine inhibitors? Recalling the previous two slides, answer on your own.

The timeline of the neutrophil and the macrophage. Neutrophils appear at the focus first, a few minutes after an inflammatory stimulus; they are regarded as the first phagocytes. Macrophages arrive after a few hours and remain longer at the focus of infection. In an uncontrolled response, in both cell types excess mediators, that is, cytokines, ROS and NO, damage the host cells.

Adhesion and migration proceed in sequence. First, TNF-α and IL-1 induce expression of adhesion receptors on the endothelium and the neutrophil. Selectin activators such as histamine and thrombin facilitate the initial contact and rolling of the leukocyte, that is, selectins ensure rolling. Then ICAM and integrins provide firm adhesion. Chemotaxis is carried out through fMLP, C5a, PAF, LTB4 and IL-8; they activate the neutrophil. Finally, the cell migrates into the tissue.

Neutrophil priming, that is, pre-sensitisation. A neutrophil in the blood is resting, activated or primed; a primed cell responds to a stimulus much more strongly. Among endogenous factors, TNF-α gives the strongest priming. Exogenous factors: bacterial LPS, fMLP and opsonin-coated pathogens. TNF-α or LPS, through p38 MAPK, increase flavocytochrome b558 in the membrane and thereby enhance the respiratory burst. A primed granulocyte releases excess ROS and cytokines, and its apoptosis slows; this can lead to lipid peroxidation and DNA mutations.

Neutrophil apoptosis and necrosis. A resting neutrophil lives for about 8 hours; activators such as LPS prolong its life. Regulatory T cells, that is, Treg, suppress the formation of reactive oxygen species in the neutrophil and induce apoptosis. The effect of Treg is exerted through perforin and granzyme, and through Fas and FasL; LPS enhances this effect. Compare apoptosis and necrosis. In apoptosis the cell controls the process itself, no toxic contents are released, there is no damage to the surroundings, chromatin condenses and DNA fragments. Necrosis, by contrast, is uncontrolled death: the cell contents spill out and may damage the tissue.

t: Neutrophil cytokines: immunoregulatory and reparative role
n: Neutrophil cytokines play an immunoregulatory and reparative role. Neutrophils synthesise proinflammatory cytokines: IL-1α, IL-1β, IL-6, IL-7, IL-18 and MIF; and also anti-inflammatory cytokines: IL-1ra, TGF-β1, TGF-β2. Immunoregulatory cytokines: IFN-β, IL-12, IL-21, IL-23, IL-27; colony-stimulating factors: G-CSF, GM-CSF, SCF. Angiogenic and fibrogenic factors VEGF, FGF2, TGF-α, HGF, CC and CXC chemokines, as well as members of the TNF family, that is, TNF-α, FasL, TRAIL, APRIL and RANKL, are also produced. Therefore, in addition to killing microbes, the neutrophil displays immunomodulatory and reparative properties; the mechanisms of cytokine expression are not fully understood.

t: Case analysis: cytokines high at a late stage
n: Case analysis. Situation: high cytokine levels were found in the blood of patients diagnosed with septic shock. The reason is that studies are often performed when shock has already developed; the high level is the result of microbial multiplication and persistence of bacterial antigens. Model: if cytokines are few at the beginning, bacteria multiply without being completely eliminated; then massive cytokine activation leads to SIRS and septic shock. Question: why did anti-TNF-α therapy, that is, treatment against tumour necrosis factor-α, give little benefit in such patients?

Link between endothelium and coagulation. The cytokines TNF-α and IL-1 increase expression of tissue factor, that is, TF, on the endothelium. The coagulation cascade runs as follows: through TF factor VII is activated, then factor X is activated, prothrombin is converted to thrombin, and fibrinogen to fibrin. In septicaemia fibrinolysis weakens while coagulation continues; as a result, coagulopathy develops. Thrombosis of the microcirculation aggravates organ damage; disseminated intravascular coagulation, that is, DIC, may develop.

Nitric oxide, NO, a two-faced mediator. NO is synthesised continuously from L-arginine, molecular oxygen and NADPH with the participation of the enzyme NOS. Constitutive NOS is present in neurons and endothelium; iNOS is transient and increases under the influence of cytokines. NO kills microbes, but in septic shock its excess causes hypotension and damage. The pathway is as follows: the cytokines TNF-α and IL-1 increase, iNOS expression rises, much NO is formed, peroxynitrite is formed, and the respiratory chain and the Krebs cycle are blocked.

t: Protein C and the anticoagulant system
n: Protein C and the anticoagulant system. Protein C is formed mainly in the liver; under the action of the thrombin–thrombomodulin complex and protein S it is converted to activated protein C, that is, APC. APC reduces thrombin by inactivating factors Va and VIIIa; by inactivating PAI-1 it supports fibrinolysis; it also inhibits TNF and NF-κB synthesis and leukocyte adhesion. Inflammation reduces protein C activation. In severe sepsis, protein C was low in 85% of patients; a low level has been reported as a predictor of death. Recombinant human APC, that is, drotrecogin α, was an adjunctive treatment in severe sepsis but did not affect survival; in children, intracranial haemorrhage increased and the trial was stopped.

Quick questions on the endothelium and NO. First question: what do TF and tPA do? Answer: TF initiates coagulation through factor VII; tPA forms plasmin from plasminogen and ensures fibrinolysis. Second question: what happens if iNOS is activated in septic shock? Answer: NO increases greatly and severe hypotension resistant to treatment develops. Third question: what happens if APC is deficient in sepsis? Answer: coagulation intensifies and fibrinolysis slows; microthrombosis and MODS develop. Attention: constitutive NOS is not iNOS. The former is constantly present in neurons and endothelium; iNOS is transient and, under the influence of cytokines, increases in macrophages and activated endothelium.

t: Case analysis: DIC and lung injury
n: Case analysis. A patient with severe sepsis shows signs of microthrombosis and, at the same time, bleeding; lung function is worsening. Cytokines enhance coagulation and weaken natural fibrinolysis; thrombosis appears in the microcirculation and organ injury increases. In DIC, that is, disseminated intravascular coagulation, coagulation and bleeding occur at the same time; it is difficult to balance these opposing processes during treatment. Question: why is the lung the organ most often damaged in SIRS? Hint: blood flow, the microvascular network, perfusion pressure and macrophages.

Respiratory burst and NADPH oxidase. An activated neutrophil sharply increases its consumption of O2; this is called the respiratory burst. NADPH oxidase, that is, nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate oxidase, converts O2 to the superoxide anion. At rest the components are separated, so the enzyme is inactive; on activation they assemble in the membrane. The chain: the neutrophil is activated by cytokines, p47 is phosphorylated via PKC, p40, p47 and p67 move to the membrane, bind to b558, to p22 and gp91, and superoxide is formed from O2 using NADPH.

Reactive oxygen species. ROS are molecules with one or more unpaired electrons, and therefore highly reactive. They peroxidise lipids, damage nucleic acids and inactivate enzymes. The half-life of ROS is very short; they are difficult to track in a living organism. Superoxide is formed from O2 by NADPH oxidase and, through dismutase, SOD, is converted to H2O2. H2O2 itself is weakly active and is activated on a metal ion. The hydroxyl radical is formed from Fe2+ in the Fenton reaction; it is extremely reactive and damages lipids and DNA. Hypochlorous acid is formed from H2O2 and Cl− by myeloperoxidase and forms chloramines with amines.

t: Lipid peroxidation and the antioxidant barrier
n: Lipid peroxidation and the antioxidant barrier. The greatest change occurs in the lipid part of the membrane: peroxidation proceeds non-enzymatically under the action of Fe2+ or enzymatically via lipoxygenase and cyclooxygenase. A small amount of ROS is enough to start it, because the process is self-propagating. Attention: an aldehyde is not a free radical; it is less reactive and therefore spreads far. Aldehydes are “secondary messengers”: they react with the thiol and amine groups of proteins, change their antigenicity, stop the enzyme and break the DNA strand. Antioxidant barrier: SOD converts superoxide to H2O2, glutathione, GSH, neutralises H2O2; vitamin E protects the membrane, and vitamin C restores it.

Ischaemia-reperfusion and xanthine oxidase. Reperfusion is a complication of shock that proceeds with ARDS, that is, respiratory distress, and MODS, that is, multiple organ dysfunction. In healthy tissue dehydrogenase predominates; in anoxia it converts to xanthine oxidase, XO, and forms superoxide. The chain: in ischaemia, tissue hypoxia, dehydrogenase converts to xanthine oxidase; in reperfusion oxygen returns, XO forms superoxide from O2, then ROS, NO and neutrophils aggravate the damage. XO is the main source of ROS after reperfusion.

Case analysis. In a patient in shock, circulation was restored, and then signs of lung injury, that is, ARDS, and organ dysfunction, that is, MODS, intensified. In hypoxic tissue, in the intestinal villi, liver and lungs, dehydrogenase converted to xanthine oxidase; when oxygen returned, it produces superoxide. Neutrophils release O2− through NADPH oxidase in the “respiratory burst”; mitochondria and endothelium also produce a large part of the ROS. Question: what are the sources of ROS in this patient? Name xanthine oxidase, neutrophil NADPH oxidase, mitochondria and endothelium, and explain how they amplify one another.

The difference between PAMP and DAMP in trauma SIRS. SIRS, that is, systemic inflammatory response syndrome, is a non-specific excessive defensive response to a stressor. In infectious SIRS the signal is PAMP, the source is microbes and infection, the receptor is PRR, and the immune system is activated. In trauma SIRS the signal is DAMP, the source is injured tissue and mitochondria, and the same PRRs, that is, TLR and NLR, are involved. The initial death is called the “first hit”; SIRS and MODS, that is, multiple organ dysfunction syndrome, are the “second hit”.

t: mtDNA signalling pathways: TLR9, cGAS-STING, NLRP3
n: mtDNA signalling pathways. mtDNA, that is, mitochondrial DNA, is recognised as foreign because of unmethylated CpG repeats. The first pathway is TLR9: through MyD88 it switches on the nuclear factor NF-κB and increases synthesis of TNF-α, IL-1β and IL-6. The second pathway is cGAS–STING, that is, cyclic GMP-AMP synthase and stimulator of interferon genes: through cGAMP STING is activated, IRF3 and NF-κB are triggered, and type I interferon and cytokines are induced. The third pathway is the NLRP3 inflammasome: oxidised mtDNA activates caspase-1, IL-1β and IL-18 are formed, and pyroptosis occurs.

mtFP and other mtDAMPs. mtFP, that is, mitochondrial formyl peptides, are synthesised from mtDNA; in trauma they enter the blood and attract immune cells through FPR1–FPR3, that is, formyl peptide receptors. FPR1 enhances chemotaxis, degranulation, ROS and cytokine formation in neutrophils; mtFP is a single common ligand for all human FPRs. When TFAM, that is, mitochondrial transcription factor A, is damaged, mtDNA is released; it is itself also a DAMP. mtRNA causes inflammation through TLR8, MyD88 and the RIG-I pathway. If cardiolipin is exposed on the outside, mtDNA is released and switches on cGAS–STING; ATP raises IL-1β, IL-6 and TNF-α; cytochrome c acts through TLR4 and NF-κB.

Effects of mtDAMPs in organs. In the lung the mtFP–FPR1, mtDNA–cGAS/STING and NLRP3 pathways operate, and plasma mtDNA is related to the severity of ARDS. In the kidney RIP3 and PGAM5 lead to release of mtDNA, cGAS/STING participates, and within 48 hours mtDNA and AKI, that is, acute kidney injury, are associated. In the cardiovascular system there are mtFP–FPR and endothelial dysfunction; in a shock model NO release and hypotension were observed. In the brain mtDNA acts through NLRP3, cGAS/STING and microglia, and cerebrospinal fluid mtDNA is related to severity. In the liver, oxidised mtDNA activated Kupffer cells through NLRP3 and aggravated liver injury; this is a rat model. In intestinal ischaemia-reperfusion, epithelial mtDNA amplifies inflammatory cytokines through the TLR9 pathway. The plasma mtDNA level predicts the risk of SIRS after trauma with moderate accuracy.

Quick questions on trauma and mtDAMPs. First question: is sterile SIRS in trauma driven more by PAMPs or by DAMPs? Answer: mainly by DAMPs, including mitochondrial DAMPs, that is, mtDAMPs. Second question: which receptor does mtDNA activate? Answer: TLR9 binds unmethylated CpG DNA and triggers the NF-κB and MAPK pathways. Third question: to which receptor do mitochondrial formyl peptides bind? Answer: FPR; FPR1 and FPR2 are found most often on neutrophils. Attention: PAMP is not DAMP. A PAMP is a microbial molecule; a DAMP is a molecule released from the host's own cell. Mitochondria are bacteria-like, which is why mtDAMPs resemble PAMPs.

Case analysis. In a polytrauma patient, the plasma mtDNA level on admission is much higher than in healthy people. Mitochondria are damaged and mtDAMPs have entered the blood. In the source, those with high blood mtDNA 2 hours after trauma had a high risk of MODS, that is, multiple organ dysfunction syndrome. The level continued to rise up to 24 hours. Discussion: what does this biomarker reflect? It reflects mitochondrial damage and DAMP load and signals the risk of SIRS and MODS. The authors stress that additional clinical studies are needed before mtDNA can be used as a biomarker. The cut-off value is not given in the source.

Lung morphology: stages of DAD. The first, exudative or acute stage lasts 0–7 days: oedema, neutrophils and hyaline membranes. In the second, proliferative stage, from day 3–7, type II pneumocyte hyperplasia is observed. In the third, fibrotic or chronic stage, on day 14 extensive fibroblasts, collagen and fibrosis appear. The hyaline membrane is important for DAD; if the injury is less than 24 hours old, changes may be minimal. Type II pneumocyte hyperplasia begins on days 2–3 and by day 7 is extensive; atypia may be present. Attention: DAD is a histological pattern, whereas ARDS is a clinical syndrome; one can occur without the other.

t: Type II pneumocyte hyperplasia and the mechanism of fibrosis
n: Type II pneumocyte hyperplasia and the mechanism of fibrosis. Hyperplasia is an increase in cell number together with hypertrophy; atypia may be present, that is, cytomegaly, karyomegaly and multinucleated cells. It begins 2–3 days after injury and is extensive by day 7; solitary hypertrophic pneumocytes mimic a reactive macrophage, and the cytokeratin IGK distinguishes them. The chain: type II pneumocytes and macrophages are damaged and release TGFβ, which activates myofibroblasts and fibroblasts that deposit collagen. In fibrosis, fibroblasts and myofibroblasts infiltrate the septa and the alveolar fibrin. If repair does not occur, lung function is permanently reduced.

ARDS endotypes and their mechanism. Five endotypes are distinguished: epithelial, endothelial, local inflammation, angiopathy and systemic inflammation. In the epithelial endotype the alveolar epithelium is injured, fluid clearance is impaired and oedema appears. In the endothelial endotype the vascular barrier is disrupted, and neutrophil sequestration and coagulation occur. In local inflammation, injury of the airways and interstitium spreads, neutrophils accumulate and oxidative damage occurs. In systemic inflammation, a systemic insult such as sepsis or pancreatitis leads to endothelial apoptosis and a prothrombotic state. Angiopathy: vasoconstriction and microthrombi; it relies mainly on COVID-19 angiopathy in humans. The idea: the primary injury leaves a specific molecular signature; this helps precision treatment.

t: Systemic inflammation endotype: sepsis and SIRS
n: Systemic inflammation endotype: sepsis and SIRS. In SIRS the endothelium is widely activated; the risk of circulatory disturbance rises. Oxidative stress makes the endothelium prothrombotic and increases capillary permeability. Cytokines increase, complement C3a and coagulation are activated; neutrophil apoptosis is weakened. The chain: in sepsis or SIRS systemic mediators appear, the endothelium is damaged, vascular permeability increases, oxidative stress and cytokines intensify, and finally pulmonary oedema, that is, ARDS, develops.

Immunomodulation: MSC and IL-6 blockers. Mesenchymal stromal cells, MSC, home to the damaged endothelium, repair the tissue and restrain inflammation; the risk is thromboembolism. Tocilizumab is an antibody against the IL-6 receptor: it blocks the IL-6 receptor and relieves the manifestations of the cytokine storm; side effects and infection risk were not increased. Anakinra is an IL-1 receptor antagonist that reduced mortality in COVID-19. Risk: thromboembolism with MSC infusion; in systemic inflammation, efficacy has not yet been proven and trials are awaited.

t: Case analysis: pancreatitis and respiratory failure
n: Case analysis. Dogs with acute pancreatitis: of 109 dogs, 33 had respiratory signs and 3 had veterinary ARDS, that is, acute respiratory distress syndrome. In the blood, antithrombin was reduced, while TNF, that is, tumour necrosis factor, IL-6 and C-reactive protein were increased, which is a sign of systemic inflammation. In humans, of 359 cases of acute pancreatitis, 31, that is, 9%, had respiratory failure; ARDS usually developed on days 2–7. Question: which endotype? Answer: the systemic inflammation endotype, that is, mediators from a distant focus arrive with the blood and damage the pulmonary endothelium.

Let us conclude. In SIRS, cytokines disrupt the endothelium and enhance coagulation; disseminated intravascular coagulation, DIC, and multiple organ dysfunction, MODS, develop. Morphologically, diffuse alveolar damage, DAD, develops in the lung: oedema, neutrophils, hyaline membranes; then type II pneumocyte hyperplasia and fibrosis. As a biomarker, plasma mitochondrial DNA, mtDNA, rises after trauma and predicts the risk of SIRS with moderate accuracy. There are also open questions: when and which immunomodulator to apply is unknown; cytokines play both a damaging and a protective role.
